section.title: Introduction
section.content: The order in which instructions are arranged in an algorithm is very important. These instructions are executed one by one in the order they appear. An instruction in an algorithm can only be executed after the instruction that precedes it has been executed. But sometimes, certain situations require that one or more instructions be skipped in a sequence of instructions. This processing is possible thanks to conditional instructions.

bulletPoints.point: ▶️ Instructions are executed sequentially by default
🔀 Conditional instructions allow skipping or ignoring certain instructions
🔀 This chapter presents the different conditional instructions with their syntax, flowchart and examples

section.title: Importance of Conditional Instructions
section.content: To illustrate the importance of conditional instructions, let's take the example of an algorithm that calculates the inverse of a number. The following simple algorithm will cause an abnormal termination if the entered number is zero:

example.title: Inverse Algorithm (problematic)
example.point: ✏️ The computer should calculate the inverse of a number only if that number is not zero. Basic instructions (assignment, read, write) cannot respond to this need. Therefore, we need conditional instructions.

section.title: Presentation of a Condition
section.content: A condition is a logical expression of relation or boolean type. A condition always returns a result of Boolean type (True or False).
section.point: ▶️ Chaining of Comparison Operators In algorithmics, a condition cannot have two comparison operators chained together. For example, the condition (4 < a < 8) is incorrect. The correct algorithmic form is: (a > 4) and (a < 8).

section.title: Conditional Instructions
section.content: Control instructions used in algorithmics are divided into two main categories: conditional instructions and looping instructions. Conditional instructions allow you to choose between different processing, and looping instructions are used to repeat the same processing multiple times.

subsection.title: Alternatives with One or Two Choices
subsection.content: These conditional instructions are based on the execution of a single condition to choose the processing to execute. They can take two forms: simple alternative or complete alternative.

subsubsection.title: Simple Alternative (IF ... THEN)
subsubsection.content: The simple alternative is used when we want to perform a specific processing if a condition is true, and do nothing if the condition is false. The condition used is often of comparison type.

example.title: Absolute Value of an Integer
Inverse of a Number (Complete Version)

subsubsection.title: Complete Alternative (IF ... THEN ... ELSE)
subsubsection.content: The complete alternative expresses a choice between two processing: Processing 1 and Processing 2. When the condition is satisfied (TRUE), we execute Processing 1. When the condition is not satisfied (FALSE), we execute Processing 2.

example.title: Inverse of a Number with Complete Alternative

subsection.title: Alternative with Multiple Choices
subsection.content: In the case of multiple choices, it is possible to nest several simple or complete conditional instructions to form a more complex structure capable of supporting multiple choices.

example.title: Observation Based on a Student's Average

explanation.point: 🔀 Admitted if the average is greater than or equal to 10
🔀 Remedial if the average is strictly less than 10 and greater than or equal to 9.5
🔀 Failed if the average is strictly less than 9.5

subsection.title: CASE ... OF Instruction
subsection.content: This conditional instruction is also called selective choice condition. It selects between multiple choices at once, not between two alternative choices. Its particularity is the use of an arithmetic expression, unlike the previous instructions which use one or more conditions.
